newsitem.title: USA: IMF study sees big excess dollar reserves post - EMU.
newsitem.headline: IMF study sees big excess dollar reserves post - EMU.

text.p: European central banks are likely to find themselves saddled with some $105 billion worth of excess currency reserves after the launch of monetary union, a new International Monetary Fund Working Paper said.

The paper, by IMF economists Paul Masson and Bart Turtelboom, said that might lead to a tendency for the U.S. currency to depreciate over time as European Union countries trim their excess reserves, most of which would be in dollars.

However, the study said such sales were unlikely to be the dominant influence on currency rates after the launch of monetary union. Other factors, such as the monetary stance and credibility of the new European Central Bank, will have a bigger influence.
For the purposes of their estimates, the authors assumed that all 15 EU members take part in monetary union, currently scheduled to begin in January 1, 1999.

The study said the new central bank will likely be forced, at least initially, to practice a reasonably discretionary monetary policy. That is partly because the bank will find it hard to set targets for money supply because of uncertainties surrounding demand for the new European currency, the euro.
According to the authors, the central bank might thus opt to focus more attention on the euro's value on the foreign exchange market in setting monetary policy.

"One indicator that might be given prime attention is the exchange value of the euro," the paper said, adding, "The exchange rate is a particularly visible and publicly recognized indicator and ... will have a clear interpretation for the general public."

The authors played downs fears that the launch of monetary union will hinder policy coordination among major nations, arguing that such coordination would help Europe deal with the many uncertainties facing it.
